rv.q: A show like Vanya telescopes the empathy at the core of theater'

As adapted by Simon Stephens, 'Vanya' is deeply serious and generally faithful in its engagement with Chekhov, offering not just a modernized gloss on the play's language and settings but also a new way of seeing into the heart of its beauty.
Scott...his rippling, androgynous energy, is a fearlessly sensual actor
It's a bewitching collaboration between actor and audience, storytelling that seems to skate effortlessly on a frozen lake of shared imagination.

Vanya could have been a stunt but, instead, we're treated to the spectacle of a fine actor testing his talent against one of the theatre's greatest texts, applying a startlingly successful form of cinematic naturalism as he immerses himself fully in each character.
Vanya, is, of course, more than a fresh interpretation of a classic play. It is an event and one that shouldn't be missed.
To watch Scott in Vanya is to experience his top-tier acting talents at full force.
Olivier Award winner Scott takes great care to assign a distinct voice and defining mannerisms to each role... He's a marvel.
Regardless, witnessing Scott's excellence within the relative intimacy of a 299-seat playhouse is a treat.
The result is an immersive tone poem of regret, beautifully acted but emotionally diffuse.
Vanya is a practically impressive but theatrically mixed experience.
Perhaps it's too much to ask that a production tell a cogent story of a classic play when there's only one actor playing nine characters and the usual running time has been cut almost in half.
I was just not sure why he is performing a one-man Vanya, other than to impress us by pulling it off.
The play is the not-to-be-missed 'Vanya' playing at the Lucille Lortel only through Sunday, May 11, 2025.

cn.t: Critics praise Andrew Scott's astonishing virtuoso performance in this one-man adaptation of Chekhov's classic, with reviewers highlighting his remarkable ability to embody all characters and the production's witty, wrenching staging.
